D017_l001.question: A 31-year-old single male working as an air traffic controller presents with a persistent preoccupation regarding the appearance of his facial features, particularly the shape of his nose, which clinical examination reveals to be within normal anatomical limits. He reports recurrent, intrusive thoughts about these perceived facial flaws, which have become a source of significant psychological distress. Over the past several years, he has pursued multiple dermatological interventions and consultations with plastic surgeons in attempts to correct these concerns, despite minimal or no objective physical abnormalities. These behaviors have consumed considerable time and have contributed to disruptions in occupational functioning, including difficulty maintaining focus during work shifts and increased absenteeism. The patient spends excessive amounts of time each day scrutinizing his appearance in mirrors and comparing his features to others. There is no evidence of psychotic symptoms, and insight into the nature of his concerns is limited. Mood disturbances, including symptoms of anxiety and low self-esteem, are present but are secondary to the central preoccupation. The course of the condition has been chronic, with symptoms persisting for several years and resulting in clinically significant impairment in daily functioning.
D017_l001.options:
A. Bulimia Nervosa
    B. Body Dysmorphic Disorder
    C. Bipolar II Disorder
    D. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

D017_l002.question:

There is a documented history of repeated dermatological interventions and consultations for surgical augmentation aimed at altering body contour, which she sought in an effort to achieve her desired physique. These procedures have provided only transient relief, with ongoing dissatisfaction leading to further planned interventions.

Significant functional impairment is evident, including difficulties maintaining personal relationships and disruptions in work schedule due to time spent on appearance-related behaviors. There is no indication that her divorce, which occurred six years prior to symptom onset, contributed causally to her presentation. The patient exhibits no overt delusions, though the beliefs are held with poor insight. Mood and anxiety symptoms are present but appear secondary to appearance-related distress.

A. Bulimia Nervosa
